the variance in height and BMI is explained by ∼45% and ∼17%, respectively, of common SNPs, and that the variance explained per chromosome is proportional to chromosome length.

the variance explained for height, BMI, QTi and von Willebrand Factor by common SNPs is approximately 50% (45%, 17%, 21% and 25%, respectively), and that this is proportional to the length of the chromosome.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the partitioning of genetic variance for complex traits using genome-wide SNP data.

the genetic basis for variation in human height, body mass, blood clotting and heart rhythm, and we have developed new methods to estimate the extent to which these traits can be explained by common variants in the human genome.
the genetic architecture of complex traits and how it can be estimated from genome-wide association data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the heritability of a trait is a function of the total number of genes involved, the number of alleles at each of these genes and their effect size.

common SNPs explain a substantial fraction of the variation for these traits, but the majority is still unexplained and is most likely due to rare variants and/or interactions between common and rare variants and/or epistatic interactions.
the majority of heritability in height, BMI and von Willebrand Factor is captured by common variants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
common SNPs explain a substantial amount of genetic variation for height (45%), BMI (17%), von Willebrand Factor (25%) and QTi (21%).

common genetic variants contribute to the majority of genetic variance for these complex traits, but that the genetic architecture for these traits is highly complex and that there are many genes of small effect.
the heritability of complex traits is not due to rare variants but to the additive effect of common variants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a large proportion of the genetic variance for complex traits can be explained using common SNPs.
common SNPs can account for a substantial proportion of genetic variation for many complex traits.

a substantial amount of the variation in height, BMI and QT interval can be explained by SNPs in or around genes, and that the variance explained in each region is proportional to the length of DNA contained therein.
